items.model_answer:
Assuming you mean Princess Mary Tudor, Henry VIII’s daughter and the future Mary I, a marriage to Philip of Bavaria in the late 1530s or 1540s would probably have changed English politics less by making Mary “German” and more by preventing her later Spanish marriage to Philip II.

The biggest immediate effect would be diplomatic. Mary’s actual marriage to Philip of Spain in 1554 was deeply unpopular because many English people feared England would become subordinate to Spain and be dragged into Habsburg wars. A Bavarian or Wittelsbach husband would have been less threatening. Bavaria was important inside the Holy Roman Empire, but it was not a world power like Spain. So Mary’s marriage would likely have produced less anti-foreign panic, probably no Wyatt’s Rebellion in the same form, and less fear that England was becoming a Spanish satellite.

Religiously, Mary herself would almost certainly have remained Catholic. Her Catholicism came from her mother Catherine of Aragon, her own conscience, and her resistance to Henry VIII’s break with Rome. A Bavarian marriage would not have turned her Protestant. If she became queen, she would still likely try to restore Catholic worship and reconciliation with Rome. However, without the Spanish marriage, Catholic restoration might have looked less like a foreign project. Opposition to it may have been somewhat weaker, though Protestant resistance would still have existed. The Marian burnings might still have happened, because they were driven mainly by domestic religious policy, bishops, Parliament’s revival of heresy laws, and Mary’s own convictions, not simply by Spain.

The succession would be the crucial issue. If Mary and Philip of Bavaria had children, especially a son, Elizabeth would probably never have become queen. England might have passed into the hands of a Catholic Tudor-Wittelsbach heir. That would radically alter later history: no Elizabethan Religious Settlement as we know it, no Elizabethan Protestant identity in the same form, no Mary Queen of Scots crisis in the same way, and probably no Spanish Armada scenario as it happened. England might have remained officially Catholic for longer, though Protestantism would still have had strong support among parts of the nobility, clergy, merchants, and southeast England.

If Mary and Philip had no surviving children, the long-term result would be more limited. Mary might still become queen in 1553, restore Catholicism, and die without an heir, after which Elizabeth would still inherit. But Elizabeth’s reign would begin in a different diplomatic climate: England might not have been tied so closely to Spain, might not have entered Spain’s war against France, and therefore might have avoided or delayed the loss of Calais in 1558.

So the most likely broad outcome is this: Mary’s reign would have been less dominated by fear of Spanish influence, England might have avoided war with France and the loss of Calais, and Catholic restoration might have faced somewhat less nationalist opposition. But the truly transformative change would depend on children. A surviving child of Mary and Philip of Bavaria could have prevented Elizabeth I’s accession and changed the entire religious and dynastic direction of England.

items.question: What If Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible
human_answers: I suppose the first question is what is meant by apocrypha? Because it can mean different things and they're all different to address. Is it what many Protestants and Rabbinic Judaism call apocrypha? That is the additional books of the Old Testament that are instead considered Deuterocanon in Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy? At its core, these are books found in the LXX (Septuagint), but not found in the Masoretic text and are considered canonical texts for the majority of the Christian world. Removing the Protestant Masoretic preference resolves that part easily. Is it the broader Second Temple literature, often called Jewish Apocrypha? This is largely apocalyptic literature and includes things like Enoch, the somewhat related Jubilees, Esdras A (or III Ezra, or I Esdras...) , the Apocalypse of Esdra (IV Ezra/II Esdras), the various Baruchs, but also includes Wisdom literature like Psalms 151-155, Wisdom of Sirach, and the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs. Some of these were contained in LXX translations (Sirach, the Esdras, Psalms 151-155, etc), while others weren't (Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, II Baruch, Enoch). This is a mixed bag for canonical status, some of them made it in due to being in existing Greek collections (the LXX), while others weren't. Enoch certainly saw a lot of respect in the early church, but it ultimately lost its status over time and only remained in Ethiopia; which itself has weird canon, the Ethiopic Bible includes Enoch and Jubilees before the Esdras, and also includes the 3 Books of Meqabyan (Ethiopic Maccabees), while disincluding the actual Books of Maccabees (and the Ethiopic books are not at all related, they aren't about martyrs at all in fact, and are almost certainly written in the Middle Ages in Ge'ez originally). A lot of these are interesting books that could have significant impact on theology, but most of them are written quite late too, which was a large part of why they weren't included in any canon; most were know pseudepigrapha even at the time. Then we have the New Testament apocrypha, which ranges from things like gnostic literature and known pseudepigrapha with little chance of incorporation to the antilegomena, many of which had good chance of inclusion. Those not included, but that could have been are the Gospel of the Hebrews (scholars think there's actually 3 different works under this title, and they're all lost), the Apocalypse of Peter, the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Epistle of Barnabas and the Didache. Worth stating is that the antilegomena weren't "removed," there was heavy debate early in Christianity of what was and wasn't canonical. Different churches used different books. Some were popular in one place, but unknown in others. Worth stating for the record: the Council of Nicea had NOTHING to do with canonical formation and this was still getting discussed for centuries after. The Church Father Jerome is one of the most important figures in the Old Testament canon development, he was highly influential in the West and was one of the main reasons for why the Catholic and Orthodox Deuterocanons are slightly different. As far as the New Testament, most of the Acts of the Apostyles genre were known pseudepigrapha and very clearly non-canonical even in content. They were popular literature and very clearly derived from the Greek novel tradition. Acts of Paul being one exception to this, it was deeply popular and some argued canonical, but in a canon that includes the Pastorals (and even the Deutero-Paulines), it just didn't fit with the theology of the Pauline letters (although I'd argue it fits quite well with the Authentic Pauline corpus). The Apocylpse of Peter wasn't actually well regarded by most priests and theologians though, but it was certainly popular. Its essentially an early Dante's Inferno. The Shepherd/Hermas, Barnabas (NOT the Gospel of Barnabas, which is a medieval forgery), and the Didache I think are the easiest bunch, although not entirely without problem. The Shepherd is deeply allegorical, but was known to not be apostolic (not insurmountable, as Hebrews made it in, but apostolic lineage was important) and has an arguably binitarian lean to it. Barnabas is also allegorical and also deeply anti-jewish. It is essentially saying that the Jews misread their own books, and this is what the Jewish laws really mean - a lot of these require some serious contortion, to say the least. The Didache is interesting since its the first book of the genre of "Church Orders," which are basically moral and litergical texts. In some ways, its an early version of the genre that would become the Anglican Book of Common Prayer. Some other possibilities are the Odes of Solomon, which are a Judeo-Christian work, likely from the Qumran community, with a pretty strong connection to the Johannine literature.

Another work to consider is the Ascension of Isaiah, a christian work written as a series of visions/prophecies of the prophet Isaiah. Also, the Book of Adam and Eve could become part of the Bible, it discusses what happens to Adam and Eve after Genesis, which is interesting. I doubt the distinction of a so-called "Thomasine" branch of anything, seeing as the gospel of Thomas is a late forgery, dating from the 2nd Century, and not originating from any known centers of Christianity claiming Thomasine origin, Kerala, Edessa or Bactria. The chance of the Didache becoming part of the Bible seems slight to me, seeing as its genre isnt really saying it should be, its just a how to book, thought to be directed to clergy. I would agree the best chance to expand is going to be the Apostolic fathers works: Letters of Ignatius, Polycarp, possibly Papias' work might make it in as a supplement to Acts of the Apostles.

Something to keep in mind, is that "canon" actually has different meanings. And what you mean by "canon" could have major implications on just how big it can get. To general Protestants, the Biblical Canon means that these are only 66 divinely inspired books, period, no more, no less (the familiar Protestant Canon). The Catholic teaching is a bit more nuanced. It states that there are at least 73 divinely inspired books (which make up the Catholic Canon). This does actual leave open the possibility that there are other books that could be divinely inspire but just are not included. That said, there are some individual books that have been rule as incompatible with canon & not divinely inspired. For most of the other Christian sects, the concept of canon is a bit "fuzzier." With many of the books falling into a category that could best be described as "potentially divinely inspired, but since it we see no problems with it we don't need to bother making any further determinations". Thus they are still included in the canon list.

Yes I am including those (potentially). It's a challenge though so it's more of a "would it be realistic" thing. And no real timeline, could be very early or very late. No, as long as there is a somewhat notable text that does consider them canonical. For instance 1 Enoch is not considered orthodox by the majority of Christians but there is at least one denomination that does consider it such. I see. That does make sense. Apparently a lot of stories that have become Christian folklore (of sorts) are from books like the Infancy Gospel that are not usually considered canon, but there are traces throughout art and popular imagination (and even in Islam). Some of the non-canonical Gospels and Acts for instance, additional pseudo-Pauline epistles (and letters by other figures). Could be a fairly small but still notable enough to make it into the historical record and maybe persist as a niche sect.
items.original_question:
AHC: Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible

The definition of "apocrypha" obviously varies across denomination, e.g. 1 Enoch is canon according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church but not any other major denominations. But I'm thinking more along the lines of having some denomination which recognizes as many texts as possible which are not in every Biblical canon IOTL (and possible none), e.g. Acts of various specific figures (as distinct from Acts of the Apostles), Gospel of Thomas, etc. etc.
items.model_answer:
A Christian or post-Christian religion that incorporated as many apocrypha as possible could exist, but it would not simply be “Christianity with a bigger Bible.” It would become a much more plural, mystical, and internally tense tradition unless it created a hierarchy of authority inside its canon.

The closest historical model is the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose biblical canon is among the broadest in Christianity. It includes texts such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees, and several books not found in Catholic, Protestant, or most Orthodox Bibles. Another partial comparison is Latter-day Saint Christianity, which accepts additional scripture, though not mainly ancient apocrypha. A new “maximal apocryphal” church would go even further than either.

Such a religion would likely include the standard Old and New Testaments, the Catholic and Orthodox deuterocanonical books, the Ethiopian broader canon, Jewish pseudepigrapha such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, the Life of Adam and Eve, and many apocalypses. It might also canonize New Testament apocrypha: the Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Peter, Infancy Gospel of Thomas, Protoevangelium of James, Acts of Paul and Thecla, Acts of Peter, Apocalypse of Peter, Gospel of Nicodemus, various Marian texts, apostolic acts, and perhaps even Gnostic or quasi-Gnostic works such as the Gospel of Philip, Gospel of Truth, Apocryphon of John, and Pistis Sophia.

The main problem is that these texts do not agree with each other. Some are broadly compatible with ancient Catholic or Orthodox Christianity. Others teach very different views of creation, salvation, Jesus’ body, gender, angels, demons, sexuality, martyrdom, and the nature of God. For example, Enochic literature expands the role of angels, fallen watchers, cosmic judgment, and heavenly journeys. Marian apocrypha elevate Mary and her sacred biography. Infancy gospels depict a wonder-working child Jesus in ways that many Christians find theologically awkward. Gnostic texts often treat the material world as a trap or mistake and distinguish the highest God from the creator, which conflicts sharply with Jewish and orthodox Christian belief in one good Creator.

So the religion would have to choose one of two paths.

If it gave every apocryphal text equal doctrinal authority, the result would be highly unstable. Its theology would be contradictory: creation might be good in one text and a cosmic prison in another; Jesus might be fully incarnate in one text and only seemingly embodied in another; salvation might come through faith, sacraments, martyrdom, asceticism, secret knowledge, or angelic ascent depending on which text was emphasized. Such a church would probably be rejected by mainstream Christians as heretical or post-Christian.

If, however, it used a layered canon, it could be more coherent. It might say: the Gospels and core apostolic writings are primary; the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books are foundational; Enochic, Marian, apostolic, and apocalyptic texts are inspired but secondary; Gnostic or speculative writings are “mystical canon” to be interpreted allegorically rather than literally. This would resemble how some traditions distinguish between canonical scripture, liturgical books, writings of the fathers, and mystical theology, but it would bring many of those texts formally inside the canon.

The resulting religion would probably be strongly apocalyptic, angelological, sacramental, and mystical. It would emphasize hidden histories of heaven and hell, elaborate ranks of angels and demons, visionary ascents, sacred names, the harrowing of hell, Mary’s cosmic role, apostolic legends, and secret teachings of Jesus. It might also become more ascetic, since many apocryphal acts praise celibacy, renunciation, fasting, and martyrdom. Its Jesus would be not only the crucified and risen Messiah but also a revealer of hidden cosmic knowledge.

Institutionally, it would need powerful interpretive authorities: councils, bishops, prophets, scholars, or a magisterium capable of deciding how conflicting scriptures should be read. Without that, the canon would fragment the religion into factions, each favoring different apocrypha.

In short: a maximally apocryphal Christian canon is possible, but it would push the religion toward a broad, esoteric, post-orthodox form of Christianity. It would gain richness, mythic depth, and mystical variety, but at the cost of doctrinal simplicity and compatibility with mainstream Christian tradition.

items.question: What If Greek royal family that is ethnically Greek
human_answers: "What factors allowed the European powers to accept native princes in Serbia" is a false question because it presumes the European powers had a role in allowing native princes there to begin with. With the exception of Russia during the First Serbian Uprising, there were no other powers involved beyond the Ottomans. Had it ended with the First Serbian Uprising, whether in Ičko's Peace in 1807 or by 1813 otherwise, we would've seen the Ottomans consenting to a native prince in the region, in the form of Karađorđe, by themselves, and that'd be the end of it. Karađorđe was already attempting to consolidate power for himself in those latter years, even while he had opposition, so he was already set to be uncontested. Which brings forth two questions: had the Greeks fought alone, would it have increased the odds of a native prince being put in power, and would they have even chosen to be a monarchy? As others have argued so far, there was too much conflict between the various revolutionaries to allow for something like that, and it's also why OTL there actually wasn't a monarchy in Greece after the revolution until Greece's stability was brought under question and it was decided by the Great Powers that it should be a monarchy with a foreign prince in power to bolster it. This ignores some of the historical facts surrounding the dynastic conflict in Serbia. Obrenović didn't just decide he was going to challenge Karađorđe's claim to authority over the Serbs, he had become a leader in his own right, rallied the people to another uprising, and won, by the time Karađorđe attempted to come back. He had received what Karađorđe would've gotten had the First Serbian Uprising won, effectively, and he wasn't going to let him challenge that, least of all because of fears of what the Ottomans might do in response. Had the Greek War of Independence seen a decisively unifying leader like Karađorđe or Obrenović from its outset, there's no reason to assume that you'd have other leaders contesting their claim to power by wishing to assert themselves instead - when Karađorđe attempted to consolidate power, he received pushback on it, and it's likely a Greek-equivalent situation would see a similar conflict, where the consolidating leader would receive pushback from his revolutionary peers. But as everyone else has pointed out, revolutionary leadership was a lot more diffuse and filled with conflict, so there's no chance you'd have a unifying leader like that emerge. Really, the case of Serbia should highlight the fact that, had the Greek War of Independence not been a war for independence, but a war for greater autonomy ala the First Serbian Uprising up to 1807, in a TL where it was successful, depending on who's Sultan at the time, the same privileges extended in Ičko's Peace to the Serbs might be extended to the Greeks too, which means that the Ottomans would've demanded the Greeks decide on who to be prince among their leaders.
items.original_question:
AHC: Greek royal family that is ethnically Greek

Greece became independent from the Ottoman Empire in 1821. Two different European dynasties ruled it - the Bavarians (whose only king of Greece was the unpopular King Otto) and the Danish. Neither of these dynasties were of Greek heritage. However, there was a sizable Greek aristocracy in the Ottoman Empire, such as the Phanariotes of Constantinople. What if an ethnically Greek family (such as one of the Phanariot families) was chosen to rule Greece? Can you think of some candidates for a possible ethnically Greek royal family for 19th century Greece?
items.model_answer:
If Greece had had an ethnically Greek royal family after independence, the monarchy would probably have enjoyed stronger symbolic legitimacy, but it would not necessarily have been more stable.

In real history, modern Greece’s kings came first from Bavaria and then from the Danish Glücksburg dynasty. They were Orthodox or became associated with Greek Orthodoxy, but they were not ethnically Greek. This gave Greek republicans and nationalists an easy criticism: the monarchy could be portrayed as foreign, imposed by the Great Powers, and not fully rooted in the Greek nation.

A Greek dynasty would have changed that. A king from a prominent Greek family—perhaps a Phanariot, a military leader’s family, or a claimed Byzantine-descended house—could have presented himself as the natural continuation of Greek history, Orthodoxy, and the struggle for independence. This might have made the monarchy more emotionally acceptable to ordinary Greeks and reduced the sense that Greece was being ruled by outsiders.

But there would have been serious problems. One reason the Great Powers preferred foreign princes was that a native Greek monarch might have been tied to one faction, region, or clan. Early independent Greece was divided among local notables, military leaders, island interests, Peloponnesian factions, and foreign-aligned parties. Choosing one Greek family could have angered the others and possibly caused civil conflict. A foreign king was meant to be a neutral compromise.

A Greek royal family might also have been more aggressively nationalist. It could have pushed the “Megali Idea”—the dream of uniting all Greek-inhabited lands, including Constantinople, Asia Minor, Epirus, Macedonia, and the islands—even more strongly. That might have increased popular support, but it could also have made war with the Ottoman Empire more likely and alarmed Britain, France, Russia, and later Italy.

The biggest crises of Greek monarchy would probably still have happened in some form. The National Schism between King Constantine I and Eleftherios Venizelos during World War I was not only about ethnicity; it was about foreign policy, constitutional authority, military loyalty, and whether Greece should join the Entente. The Asia Minor Catastrophe of 1922 was also driven by strategic overreach, Turkish nationalist resistance, and shifting Great Power support. A Greek-born dynasty might have been blamed less as “foreign,” but it would still have been blamed if it presided over defeat.

So the likely result is this: an ethnically Greek royal family would have had better nationalist credentials and perhaps a somewhat better chance of survival, especially if it acted constitutionally and avoided factional politics. However, it would not automatically have saved the monarchy. Greece’s instability came from wars, military intervention in politics, constitutional disputes, foreign pressure, and social division—not just from the royal family’s ethnic origin.

In short, a Greek royal dynasty would have made the monarchy feel more “national,” but it would not have guaranteed a stronger or longer-lasting Greek kingdom. Its survival would have depended less on bloodline and more on political competence, constitutional restraint, and avoiding association with national disasters or dictatorship.

items.question: What If Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s
human_answers: Oh that's very flattering. Thank you I think the TL you're proposing is plausible and interesting re: the development of ATL Castile and Caroline War. I'm not sure the marriage with Philippa of Clarence is the way to achieve it, though. I don't share others' concerns about her inheritance, but it doesn't necessarily fit into Edward III's plans to create spheres of influence for his sons. Philippa, if she's not marrying Mortimer (who had some smaller land claims in Ireland before inheriting the Burke estates through Philippa) would seem to make more sense for a Fitzgerald or Butler or a knight of the Garter who Edward wanted to establish as a peer without alienating anything from the crown. You could argue that I am overestimating the importance of these spheres of influence. (This is around the time that Lionel gets a Visconti bride -- an arrangement negotiated to put pressure on the papacy to approve the Langley-Flanders marriage, which demonstrates that Edward III still had an overarching and interconnected dynastic plan.) But this is a period in which the Black Prince set out his own foreign policy. He does not simply rubber-stamp his father's agreements. It is TBP's decision to end the Castilian alliance when Pedro executed the prisoners from Nájera. Just a few years later, TBP vetoed his father's alliance with Charles the Bad. All of which is to ask, how would it matter to the Black Prince that his niece is queen of Castile? Or would TBP end the alliance anyway if Pedro acts the way he did in OTL? Then there is also the issue of Pedro's not-great treatment of his wives. We don't know much about Lionel (relative to his four more famous brothers), but we see Edward III and Gaunt have very close relationships with their daughters. Edward made his favorite daughter one of the greatest landholders in England and Gaunt was so fond of his eldest daughter (apparently because she reminded him of his late first wife) that he didn't marry her off until her mid 20s. If Lionel has this sort of affection for Philippa then he may not be willing to entrust his daughter to a king like Pedro. (Though, honestly, I think this is a less important point. Not only only is it entirely speculative of Lionel's personal affections, but Lionel does demonstrate a commitment to his father's plans in going through with the Visconti match for the main purpose of furthering his brother's marriage prospects in Flanders. Still, I don't thin Pedro's treatment of his wives can be entirely discounted.) I very strongly suspect that the marriage contract handed the Ulster estate over to Lionel in its entirety and entailed it to his heirs, regardless of remarriage. Heiresses in weak negotiating positions often lost everything to their husbands and, considering both that a) Elizabeth de Burgh only became an heiress because her father was assassinated by his cousin -- i.e., the man who would inherit if Elizabeth did not -- and b) that Elizabeth's guardian was her mother, Maud of Lancaster, who was a member of the English royal family herself, it just seems very likely that the marriage contract gave Lionel everything. Maud was predisposed to favor the royal family as a relative herself and would be very strongly predisposed to screw over the Burghs who murdered her husband by disinheriting them in favor of Lionel.

To be fair, when the negotiations presumably happen (1366 or 1367 the latest) Philippa's father Lionel is alive, healthy and about to be married for the second time. I don’t think the perspective of Philippa inheriting his estates looks all that close at this point. Moreover, I don’t think that the perspective of Pedro potentially inheriting domains in England and Ireland should scare Edward all that much. If anything, they could potentially serve as a hook to ensure the favorable Castilian policy towards England or otherwise they can be easily confiscated (it’s not like Castile can really try retain those estates against the wishes of Plantagenets). If after Lionel dies Edward really wants to revert these estates back to the crown (although as mentioned before there are arguments for Edward not to do it), I think there is a really neat way to do it. Presumably Philippa’s dowry however large can it be (BTW how large can it be? Up to £10,000 perhaps?) would not be enough to pay for Black Prince’s army (even if ITTL Edward, helping the future husband of his niece, can be a bit more moderate in his pricing). While Pedro can raise some money on his own (he was ready to pay de Guesclin 200000 gold coins – presumably florins - in 1369, so he had some money, although of course it wouldn’t be enough to settle his OTL bill with Edward), he would probably still need to pledge some his territories in lieu of the rest of the payment. So, after Philippa inherits her father’s estates, the mortgage can be rearranged with English and Irish estates now serving as a collateral instead of Castilian territories. Or even perhaps these estates can be given to the Black Prince staight away in lieu of the rest of the debt. @material_boy , what do you think about the proposed PoD and some of its consequences? I have been toying with the victorious Pedro for several years now, but the perspective of modeling the alternative HYW always seemed to daunting. It was your amazing TL that inspired me to approach it. So your opinion would be especially appreciated (although of course I would be happy to hear feedback from everyone).
items.original_question: What if Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s UPD: I have updated both the PoD and who is the most likely bride for Pedro. See up-to-date details here and further ( link ). However all the potential consequences of Pedro surviving described in the second part of this message are still very much valid. UPD 2: Please find the TL draft for 1362-1364 in this message ( link ) I've always had a soft spot for Pedro the Cruel (aka Pedro the Just) of Castile. His victory over Henry of Trastamara would have monumental consequences both for Iberian Kingdoms and for Europe in general (I will list some of them further down). While there are a few threads on the forum discussing the possibility of his victory over Henry they are all rather short and usually either discuss earlier PoDs (e. g. Joan of England surviving and marrying Pedro) or more decisive battle of Najera (with Henry being killed or captured in battle). The former is definitely plausible, but would alter 1350s and 1360s quite a bit, while the later doesn’t strike me as all that consequential (after all in 1367 Henry has a son as well as two brothers who could potentially lead the Trastamara party to victory even without Henry). IMHO the main reason for Pedro losing the Castilian Civil War were not particular mistakes on his part or successful moves on Henry’s, but rather the military dominance of du Guesclin’s routier army over Castilian one. So, if we want Pedro to retain his throne, we need to either occupy or counterbalance routiers until the Caroline Phase of the Hundred Years’ War starts. The latter was successfully done IOTL with the help of Edward the Black Prince in 1367, but the relations between Pedro and Edward quickly deteriorated mainly because Edward didn’t receive his pay as per treaty of Libourne and thus Pedro was left to his own devices in 1368-1369 and was defeated and killed. Presumably Pedro didn’t pay Edward simply because he was unable to raise such an enormous sum. The PoD I present is Pedro marrying Philippa of Clarence as part of negotiations with English. Philippa is the eldest granddaughter of Edward III and has just reached marriageable age in 1367. IOTL, she married Edmund Mortimer but of course king of Castile is a way more prestigious match (there are conflicting records about when exactly Philippa was betrothed to Edmund IOTL, but for the purpose of this PoD let us pick the latest option 1368). Pedro on the other hand is in his thirties, has not legitimate issue and both his wife and his beloved mistress are dead since 1361. The purpose of the marriage is twofold: firstly, to bring Castile closer to England and secondly to be a neat way to subsidize Edward’s expedition. I am not sure how large Philippa’s dowry was IOTL, but presumably if she has a royal marriage, it definitely should be quite large. So Edward’s army can at least partly be subsidized with his niece’s dowry. I am not sure if such an arrangement is plausible, but if it does happen consequences are massive. Presumably if the relationship between the Black Prince and Pedro is unstrained (or at least is significantly better than IOTL), the second invasion of Henry and de Guesclin would seem futile and probably doesn’t happen. In 1369 the Caroline Phase begins (even if IOTL Charles V summoned Edward because he already realized that Castille would fall to Henry, which is debatable, ITTL Charles presumably understands that Edward would help Pedro no matter what and thus he might as well go on with his plan). Thus, Henry would have very little military support and will stand no chance against Pedro and his allies. Possible consequences of the PoD: 1. Castille itself has a radically different social structure. a. IOTL Henry and his heirs had to give out large parts of royal domain for their supporters from lesser nobility that formed new aristocratic elites (since pedristas were active until mid-1380s Trastamaras needed their continous support for an extended period of time and thus royal domain suffered greatly). Quoting from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: The new dynasty came to power having given lavish grants and titles to supporting nobles, and territorial concessions to their royal allies in France and the Crown of Aragon. Henry II’s initial hold on the crown was a tentative one. New men came to the fore demanding a share of the victory, and the king also granted them substantial privileges and lands. Historians have long argued that the first decades of Trastámara rule witnessed the disappearance of the old nobility, a nobility dating to the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, and its replacement by a new nobility. In reality, the transformation was signaled by the rise to prominence of lesser branches of the great old noble houses, with a few new lesser nobles rising to very high status. This promotion in rank was tied to the granting of large estates and to extensive royal privileges. Such erosion of the royal domain and authority had, in turn, disastrous consequences for Castile over the next hundred years. Not unlike France or England in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the rise of the nobility led to waves of violence and instability. Securely grounded in their new economic power and high standing, the Castilian nobility challenged royal authority and even coveted, as was the case in the reigns of John II and Henry IV, the control of the Crown. Pedro unlike Henry is a legitimate king and thus doesn’t need such drastic measures to obtain necessary support. b. In the first half of XIV century one of the main pillars of royal power was municipal nobility (or more precisely non-noble municipal knights). At first kings bought their support against magnates by granting municipal knights’ extensive privileges, but since the latter felt constant pressure by disenfranchised bourgeoisie, they continuously welcomed royal entrenchment in cities and thus by 1340s urban centers were under firm royal control. Once again, quote from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: In less than 50 years the non-noble knights monopolized municipal offices in most Castilian cities, bought most of the land around the cities, and gained control, as they did in Burgos and Avila, of the most important ecclesiastical benefices. In return the king hoped for, and often received, their military support against the magnates and access to the cities’ fiscal resources. Moreover, as the non-noble knights gained control of their respective cities, they came into conflict with those below them. Pressured from below by the disfranchised petite bourgeoisie, the non-noble knights welcomed royal interference in the affairs of the cities and, by the 1340s, the takeover of municipal administration by royal officials (the regimiento) became a political reality. For a brief period, royal control of the urban centers became one of the most significant gains of the Castilian monarchy, but then the disorders of the late fourteenth century weakened royal control anew. IOTL many cities supported Pedro against Henry and thus were severely punished by victorious Trastamaras which greatly weakened both cities themselves and royal control over them. Thus, if Pedro retains his throne Castile is a lot more centralized with a strong royal power based on resources from a reasonably large royal domain as well as prosperous cities under firm royal control which is a stark contrast to magnate-dominated early Trastamara Spain. 2. Pedro IOTL had a firm alliance with Portugal. His uncle Pedro of Portugal helped him in his wars against both Peter of Aragon and Henry of Trastamara. When Pedro of Castile was slain, it was Portugal that was the main base for anti-Trastamara action in Iberia. Ferdinand of Portugal, Pedro of Castile’s cousin waged several wars against Trastamaras (first claiming the crown of Castile in his own right, later supporting John of Gaunt’s claim). Pedro of course is a very strong clamant to Portuguese throne in his own right, but he can further cement his claim by marrying Beatrice of Portugal to his son (who presumably should be born in early to mid 1370s roughly similarly to OTL Roger Mortimer birth date and thus ideally match Beatrice). Moreover, before Trastamara coup Portugal and Castile had the same allies and aligned economic interests (both benefited greatly from maritime trade between Northern Europe and Mediterranean, both had Genoa as a most important trade partner and England as a main ally outside of Iberia). IOTL when Portuguese interregnum happened the nobility was split with a significant portion of it supporting Trastamara claim. It were municipal elites of 4 main Portuguese cities (Lisbon, Porto, Coimba and Evora) that bankrolled anti-Trastamara faction. The main reason for these was economic (i. e. retention of profitable maritime trade with Genoa, England etc.) as well as desire to cancel Ferdinand’s pro-noble reforms (which were conducted in order to fund extremely expensive campaigns against Castille). If IOTL Pedro continues to rule Castille, Portuguese municipal elites have no reason to dislike the union with neighboring kingdom (because Ferdinan’s reforms would be unnecessary and Castile and Portugal economic and political interest would continue to be closely aligned) and thus we can encounter Castilian-Portugese union in 1380s. 3. Pedro had an advantage in the War of Two Peters against Peter of Aragon. Presumably if Henry of Trastamara is no longer a threat, he can continue pressing Aragon for economic, political (most important one being the termination of Trastamara support) and perhaps even territorial concessions (getting back Alicante, Elche and Orihuela as part of kingdom of Murcia) 4. If Pedro marries Philippa, presumably John Gaunt and Edmund Langley would have alternative brides. IOTL the marriages happened to establish a claim over kingdom of Castile. ITTL Pedro would have legitimate heirs related to English royal family without such a match and thus daughters of Peter with at best debatable legitimacy are not ideal brides for English prices. Does anybody have suggestions who John and Edmund would marry in such a scenario? 5. Perhaps the most consequential consequence of the PoD is alternative Caroline Phase of HYW. The battle of La Rochelle that crippled English fleet IOTL was won by Castilian navy. If Castile continues to be an English ally, Castilian navy either doesn’t participate or participates on English side. Thus, English are able to get significant reinforcements to Poitou and Saintonge as well as £12,000 that were supposed to be used to pay for service of local troops (IOTL this booty fell to the hands of Castilians). This potentially a least allows English to retain control over Poitou, Saintonge and Angoumois and perhaps even reverse some French gains made in previous years. Moreover with English fleet still dominating the waters around France, the main reason for the disastrous Great Chevauchee of 1373 is gone. ITTL, it makes a lot more sense to bring reinforcements by see, as was done in previous years. Thus, the Caroline Phase of HYW can be radically altered in 1372-1373, perhaps to the extent of it being a draw rather than decisive French victory. All these consequences seem rather juicy, but I am not sure if the marriage of Pedro and Philippa is all that plausible. What do you guys think? (of course if you have comments on consequences of PoD rather than the PoD itself, I would be happy to hear those too).
items.model_answer:
If Peter of Castile married an English princess in the 1360s, the most immediate effect would likely have been to make Castile a much firmer English ally during the later Hundred Years’ War. It would not automatically have saved Peter, but it could have made his survival much more plausible.

Historically, Peter’s great problem was not lack of a foreign marriage but a collapsing domestic position. He was feared and hated by many Castilian nobles, alienated important factions through executions and confiscations, and faced a serious rival in his half-brother Henry of Trastámara, who had French backing. France supported Henry partly because a pro-French Castile was strategically valuable: Castile’s navy could threaten English shipping and support French operations against Gascony.

An English marriage would have sharpened the international alignment. Peter would become not merely a useful partner of England but a dynastic ally of Edward III’s house. That would likely bring earlier and stronger English intervention on his behalf, perhaps before Henry’s invasion became overwhelming. The Black Prince did historically restore Peter after the battle of Nájera in 1367, but the alliance was transactional and broke down over money and mistrust. A royal marriage could have made that alliance more durable and harder for England to abandon.

The biggest military consequence would concern the Castilian fleet. If Peter survived as an English-aligned king, France would probably lose access to the powerful Castilian naval support it historically received under Henry II. That could significantly weaken French operations in the 1370s. In particular, the English disaster at La Rochelle in 1372, where a Castilian fleet defeated the English and helped cut off English positions in western France, might not happen or might be much less severe. English Gascony would be safer, and France’s recovery under Charles V could be slowed.

Inside Castile, however, the marriage would not erase Peter’s political weaknesses. Many nobles might see an English princess as proof that Peter was subordinating Castile to foreign interests. French agents and the Trastámara faction would exploit that. The clergy might also object depending on the exact legality of Peter’s previous marital situation, since his treatment of Blanche of Bourbon and his relationship with María de Padilla had already created serious legitimacy problems. So the marriage could strengthen Peter internationally while worsening elite resistance at home.

The most plausible short-term outcome is therefore a more intense civil war with clearer international sides: Peter backed by England and perhaps Portugal; Henry backed by France, Aragon, and anti-Peter Castilian nobles. If English aid arrived early and consistently, Peter might defeat Henry decisively and remain king. If not, the marriage would merely make his defeat more consequential, because England would have a dynastic claim or at least a stronger pretext to continue intervention.

If Peter survived and produced legitimate children with the English princess, the long-term history of Spain could change dramatically. The Trastámara dynasty might never take the Castilian throne. That would affect later Castilian politics, the succession in Aragon, and potentially the eventual union of Castile and Aragon under Ferdinand and Isabella. A pro-English Castile might orient more toward Atlantic trade and alliances with England and Portugal rather than toward France.

But if Peter were still killed, as he was historically in 1369, the result could be an even stronger English claim to Castile than the one John of Gaunt later advanced through Peter’s daughter Constance. England might support a surviving Anglo-Castilian heir, turning Castile into a prolonged arena of the Hundred Years’ War.

So, in direct terms: an English marriage in the 1360s would likely have made Peter’s regime more militarily viable and would have deprived France of one of its most valuable Iberian allies if he survived. It could have slowed French recovery in the Hundred Years’ War and prevented the rise of the Trastámara dynasty. But it would not by itself solve Peter’s domestic legitimacy crisis; without serious reconciliation with the Castilian nobility, the marriage might simply turn his civil war into a larger Anglo-French proxy conflict.

items.question: What If Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 Instead of 1492
human_answers: Lots of feedback and responses! Thank you all! I'll get to responding to other replies later on. The Crusades! That's a good point for the year 1092 and the 11th century. Also lots of good points here. Very good points. Crusader-style polities and principalities in the New World, given the attitudes of the 11th century. 1. Why wouldn't a less-weakened Muslim power establish their own colonies? As long as they're in Iberia or Morocco, they got a good chance of colonization with that geography, I think? 2. Also why not? What if the Apache or some other First Nations group taking over the North American interior, like a counterpart to the Mongols. Hopefully less bad and deadly and painful though, though that's probably too much to ask for when it comes to warfare in general. "What if the Americas were colonized by Europe beginning in 1292?" Could be worth it's own thread! Here in this one we're talking about what if 1092 instead of 1292, or OTL 1492.

That's a fun scenario to consider. One way to get Medieval America... Not sure about the naval tech of the time though. Or the ressources given the voyage between Europe and the Americas are going to be months long. These are the two crucial things that need to be fixed to get the possibility. The North Route via Greenland and Vinland probably is the best shot to make this work. Think the issue is the fact the Atlantic Ocean is pretty devoid of islands that can make effective island-hoping stops. There are the islands of Macaronesia (Azores, Canarias, Madeira, Cape Verde) close to Europe but otherwise it's a long trip until you reach the Carribeans or one of the American coasts. This isn't the same situation as the Pacific where you have tons of small islets... unless you go into ASB territory and raise the Azore plateau but that basically is making Atlantis a real thing... Naturally this situation limits the abilities of Muslim powers to colonize. Europeans at least have the Viking routes, even if that requires a successful Vinland. Though one has to remember the legend of Abu Bakr II of Mali, the most likely fictionnal predecessor of Mansa Musa. It's a stretch and we're more dealing with an African power than a European or Arabo-Muslim one, but the distance between West Africa and Brazil is a lot shorter... But then again, it's basing ourselves on a myth.

As for how would see a medieval colonization of the Americas, I would expect it happened across the Northern Atlantic and would likely focus first on the region around St Lawrence Bay, which offer several good settlements, than we would see it spread up the St, Lawrence River and later down the East Coast. Early settlements would simply be normal Norse settlements, and outside Norse settlers the main early source of “settlers” would be slaves. The need for labor would drive this slave trade and the victims of this slave trade would likely mainly come from the British islands, the Baltics, Central Europe and the post Frankish kingdoms in order of importance and it would likely disappear by the 13th century. The early settlements would likely mostly be peasants republics, as the Norse seems to mostly have established those on the frontiers. Over time we will likely see consolidation of power under large land owners both secular and ecclesia and the rise of city states. Also as the Norse runs into more powerful native societies, we may also see more centralized frontier states lead by Norse war leaders, these may also turn on the less centralized Norse states and begin to establish true kingdoms. As the population we also see the arrival of Low German merchants, who establish merchant quarters in the cities, we will likely see German artisans also moving. We could also see something like the Ashkenazi migration to Poland, but it’s more likely that Low Germans simply will fill that niche as they did in the Baltic and Nordic countries. This may result in the rise Low German city states. At the same time the Catholic Church will likely introduce more warm weather crops as the Norse moves south. As the economy of Norse America grows and expand, others will likely look into establish alternative trade route to it. Here we may see the Portuguese doing their own Columbus expedition in the early 15 century. At that point I would expect a European presence already in the Caribbean, even if it’s not fully developed. So the Portuguese establish trade routes to the Caribbean and introduce Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cash crops. We likely also see the rise off the African slave trade, but with greater European and Mestizo presence in the region already, it likely doesn’t reach OTL levels and the more traditional European structure likely means a more serfdom like structure for the African slaves. I suspect the Norse will run into the Mesoamericans in the 14th century and we will see it falling to Norse invaders or crusaders, with it being relative far away from Norse American strongholds (which will likely be the Mississippi and St. Lawrence basins and the East Coast), I expect the model of conquest will be more like the Baltic crusades. Conquest mostly by knightly monastic orders and Mexico under a knightly Grandmaster. We could easily see a repeat in the Andeans, but we could also just instead see Christian missionaries converting them.

I am not familiar with the shipbuilding industry, but I believe this is possible. There was no fundamental difference like scale or materials between shipbuilding in the 15th and 11th century. They likely needed only to devise a few new designs, or simply undertake bold try using the vessels they already have. As for the difference? An 11th-century conquest of the Americas would have been far more likely to result merely in the emergence of independent states, rather than colonies subservient to Old World powers. At best, the Italian city-states might have established a few small commercial colonies (perhaps in the Caribbean region?), but inland colonies dominating an entire continent would have been highly unlikely. This aligns more closely with the norms of that era, and the comparatively weaker commercial and artisanal capabilities of Europe would not have generated the centripetal force required to establish such a relationship; Europe could not produce so many goods that American colonists were unable to manufacture for themselves. Two rather interesting questions: 1. Could a less weakened Iberian/North African Muslim power have established its own colonies in the Americas? 2. Could a nomadic polity have been established in the North American interior?

The major issue is that open ocean travel isn't really possible before the 15th century so you'd be island hopping like the Norse did. That's certainly possible but your probably looking at a more Polynesian or Greek heroic age style model (or for that matter the Norse in Iceland and Greenland) where people are leaving to found a separate colony rather than one controlled from the Metro-pole as its to far away. Also most of the early arrivals will be in the North (Canada, then moving into New England and points south as the Little Ice age bites) and while trade webs will probably see the European diseases spread there is a good chance the native powers will have time to recover before actual Europeans reach them. That could allow the Mexican civilizations and the Inca a good chance to survive especially if they've obtained European tech in trade before the newcomers have the forces to go after them (the Aztec are probably doomed whatever as the events of OTL strongly suggest they were hated by all and someone was taking them out eventually). Also its likely they understand pretty quickly this is a new land and not a route to China (or at least not an easy one, especially once they finally sight the great desert of the Plains prairie and realize just how big America really is) so there will probably be a much stronger focus on going south to round Africa to reach the Spice islands. With actual transoceanic travel developed much earlier (and the need to improve links with the New World driving sailing tech along at a fair clip) that's likely to see Portugal starting its investigations long before Spain is finished with the Reconquista and probably with England and France nipping at her heels this time. An early rediscovery (or more dissemination of the original Norse discovery) probably doesn't completely prevent the Crusades (there is still the issue of Jerusalem) but with a bigger target for expansion and as an outlet for violence the majority of settlers will probably go there rather than the rather precarious Outremer and even if the First Crusade succeeds it may not establish an enduring polity (they had enough trouble getting immigrants as it was. Usually Europeans only went East when the states were in deep trouble). Although with a Europe that has an outlet for its expansionist desires in the Far West and doesn't feel so under siege for the first time in centuries might be able to patch things up with Islam a bit more easily. Hard to say about Religion although by 1092 the Great Schism has already happened so the Catholics will be very much the first ones there and its hard to say if there will even be a Reformation after four centuries of altered history. However if the Crusades are averted, or at least blunted there is a good chance Byzantium survives in its original form and without the damage from the Latin occupation it might be able to hold out and reform enough that they can avoid falling to the Ottoman's. Also Venice and the Italian city states may not rise as quickly if the focus on trade switches to the Atlantic (especially if the wealth of America is discovered).

items.model_answer:
If Europe had begun sustained colonization of the Americas in 1092 rather than 1492, the result would probably not have been a simple “early Spanish conquest.” Medieval Europe was too different from early modern Europe. The most likely outcome is earlier contact, disease, trade, and limited settlement first, followed only gradually by larger conquest and plantation colonies.

In 1092, Europe did not yet have the strong Atlantic monarchies, oceanic ship designs, navigational systems, gunpowder weapons, printing culture, or capitalist finance that made the 1492-era expansion so powerful. The realistic starting point would be something like an expanded Norse or North Atlantic route: Scandinavians, Normans, English, Irish, or possibly Iberian seafarers using Iceland, Greenland, and Newfoundland as stepping-stones. Colonies would likely begin along the northeast coast of North America, not immediately in the Caribbean or Mexico.

Because medieval European states were weaker, early colonization would probably be fragmented. Instead of Spain and Portugal carving up huge territories, there might be small fortified trading settlements, missionary outposts, fishing stations, and farming colonies. Europeans would trade iron tools, cloth, weapons, and livestock for furs, food, timber, and local goods. Many settlements would depend heavily on Native alliances and could be destroyed, absorbed, or forced into intermarriage and cultural blending.

The biggest and most tragic change would still be disease. Smallpox, measles, influenza, and other Old World diseases would likely spread into the Americas centuries earlier. Native American populations had no prior immunity, so epidemics could still be devastating. However, because contact in 1092 would probably be smaller and more regional than in 1492, the demographic collapse might unfold more unevenly over centuries rather than in the sudden, continent-wide shock associated with the sixteenth century.

The political map of the Americas would be very different. The Aztec Empire did not yet exist, and the Inca Empire had not yet risen. In North America, Mississippian societies were flourishing; in Mesoamerica, postclassic Maya and Toltec-influenced states were important; in the Andes, complex regional societies existed before Inca unification. Earlier European contact might prevent some later empires from forming, or it might help others form around control of European trade goods, horses, and weapons.

Horses would be especially transformative. If introduced in the twelfth century, they could spread across the Americas long before the early modern period. Plains societies in North America might become horse cultures centuries earlier. Native states could also adopt European ironworking, shipbuilding techniques, and military practices much earlier. Since Europeans in 1092 lacked firearms and large-scale imperial machinery, Native societies would have more time to adapt, making later European domination less certain and probably more contested.

Europe itself would change profoundly. American crops such as maize, potatoes, beans, squash, and tomatoes arriving in the Middle Ages could increase European food supplies centuries earlier. This might lead to faster population growth, more urbanization, and possibly earlier commercial development. But it could also intensify land pressure, warfare, and social unrest. The Black Death in the fourteenth century would still likely occur, but it would strike a Europe whose population and economy might be very different.

The balance of power inside Europe would shift toward the Atlantic earlier. England, France, Scandinavia, Portugal, Castile, and perhaps even Irish or Norman interests might gain importance sooner, while the Mediterranean-centered economy of Italian city-states and the eastern trade routes might become relatively less dominant. The Crusades, beginning in the 1090s, could also be affected: wealth, manpower, and religious energy might be diverted westward across the Atlantic rather than eastward toward the Holy Land.

Slavery and plantation agriculture might also emerge earlier, though not necessarily in the same form as after 1492. Medieval Europe already practiced slavery and serfdom, and sugar plantation systems existed in the Mediterranean. If Europeans discovered suitable American climates earlier, plantation slavery could expand centuries earlier, possibly drawing on Native labor first and African labor later. That would mean the Atlantic slave trade might begin earlier and reshape West Africa earlier as well.

Religiously, Latin Christianity would enter the Americas in the medieval rather than early modern era. Missionary activity would be tied to monasteries, crusading orders, and medieval papal authority rather than Jesuit and Franciscan missions of the sixteenth century. The Americas might become part of a medieval Christian frontier, similar in ideology to the Baltic crusades, Iberian Reconquista, or Crusader States.

Overall, the Americas would still suffer immense disruption, especially from disease, land loss, forced labor, and religious pressure. But European conquest would likely be slower, less centralized, and more dependent on Native alliances than it was after 1492. The absence of guns, mature Atlantic empires, and advanced oceanic logistics would give Native societies more time to adapt.

So the most plausible answer is: colonization in 1092 would produce an earlier but weaker Atlantic world. Disease and crops would transform both hemispheres centuries sooner; horses, iron, and Christianity would spread earlier in the Americas; Europe’s Atlantic powers would rise earlier; and slavery might expand earlier. But instead of the rapid Spanish-style conquest of vast empires, the first centuries would probably look more like scattered medieval frontier colonies, trade networks, missions, mixed societies, and long wars of adaptation.

items.question: What If an earlier, more thorough modernization of Russia
human_answers: I would highly recommend you watch NojRant's NOT the Origins of Russian Authoritarianism . If you'd like a forum post, read my posts in another thread from here onward to here : they briefly go over parts of what you're interested in, and some of it is repeated below. If you want good detail, I'd recommend Robert K. Massie's book Peter the Great . tl;dr - clothes were only a small part of the reforms, there was major modernization of the economy, education and the legal system, and you seem to have a very, very stereotyped and caricaturish understanding of the topic to speak with such confidence. The problem with the reforms was not in their superficiality, but that most of them required follow-through by Peter's successors that, for reasons I'll get into, did not happen until Catherine II some 40 years later. A highly ideological statement if ever I've heard one. Define what it means to be 'European' in clear terms. Absolutism is actually a major benefit in this situation, mainly because it is not a parliament. Parliament is essentially a tool for the ruling class to give themselves endless privileges and benefits: a ruling class composed of rural nobility would see urbanization as a threat to their power over their tenants (and ultimately their wealth) and pursue policies that deurbanize the country, whereas one dominated by bourgeois interests would be enriched by urbanization. Urbanization ultimately leads to a richer, stronger, more industrialized nation overall, while deurbanization does not. As long as Russia has a strong nobility and a comparatively weak bourgeoisie, parliament is a nonstarter for your purposes because the default net effect of parliamentary actions will be to increase nobles' control over their tenants, hence limiting urbanization, hence limiting development of private capital for industrialization. A country with no strong king to keep the nobility in check will increasingly resemble basketcases like high medieval Hungary or early modern Poland, where the nobility could ignore the king as they pleased and even fight each other as warlords ( picrel ). Even in a lesser form, this can have severe consequences: for example, under the Dual Monarchy, the Hungarian half of the empire was granted wide-ranging autonomy, which the Magyar nobility used to systematically and shortsightedly block the development of industry. The result was that Hungary remained agrarian and economically backward, even failing to compete in agriculture - the thing the Magyar nobles had sought to protect - to the extent that Russian grain imported via the Adriatic was undercutting Hungarian grain on the Austrian market. In a strong monarchy, even if the king still has to appease the nobility somewhat, he has control over the spigot of privileges and benefits and only gives them out when he has to, and expects loyal service in return - and can even retract privileges if his position is strong enough, like Ivan the Terrible did in Russia or Charles XI did in Sweden (ref. the Great Reduction ). This is constitutionally impossible with a strong parliament, though the king can always try his luck with a coup or a civil war. Even strong monarchs who retained parliaments as vestigial organs of the state, like Louis XIV, actively avoided involving them in political decisions because they knew that weak parliaments were made strong by getting involved in decisions that could've been made by the king's bureaucrats instead. However, monarchies can be weakened by unexpected deaths, child kings / regencies, changes in dynasty, coups, successful riots by the urban population against taxes, and successful rebellions by uppity nobles. These events force the king to repeal unpopular laws and grant new privileges to the nobles in exchange for their support, because his normal ability to make himself obeyed by his subjects is drastically reduced and he needs to sweeten the pot for them to obey him again. This must be avoided to preserve the king's power and prevent the nobility from pressuring him to grant more privileges. 17th century Russian tsars were weakened by the Time of Troubles, which allowed the nobility to demand a host of new concessions in exchange for their support of Mikhail Romanov as the next tsar. The most notable concession was that their pomestie fiefdoms, which were previously non-hereditary and granted to them in exchange for service to the state, were made hereditary. Russian tsars spent the next century trying to repeal these various privileges with limited success, and were occasionally hampered by new setbacks, such as the 1648 salt riot , which led to tighter restrictions on serfs being introduced to satisfy the nobility. 18th century Russian tsars were weakened by chronic succession problems, which resulted in the new tsar/tsarina having to bribe the nobility as a class with extra privileges to get them to accept their rule. The reason was that Peter had revised the succession law from male primogeniture to "Whoever the tsar chooses," meaning that the tsar's will could be forged or denied by any member of the imperial family who could bribe the palace guards to support them in a coup. If Russia had modernized earlier and more thoroughly, the most likely result is a stronger, richer, and more politically stable Russia—but not necessarily a peaceful or liberal one.

The key issue is what “modernization” means. Russia did modernize in bursts: Peter the Great westernized the army and state; Catherine expanded administration and culture; Alexander II abolished serfdom; Sergei Witte pushed railways and industry. But these reforms were often incomplete, top-down, and uneven. Russia modernized militarily and bureaucratically faster than it modernized socially, legally, or politically. Serfdom lasted until 1861, education remained limited, local self-government was weak, industrialization came late, and the autocracy resisted constitutional limits.

If Russia had abolished serfdom much earlier, expanded mass education, built reliable courts, encouraged private enterprise, developed infrastructure, and created some form of constitutional government, several major outcomes become plausible.

Russia’s economy would likely have grown faster. Earlier emancipation of the peasantry could have created a more mobile labor force, a larger domestic market, and more productive agriculture. Earlier railway construction and industrial investment would have allowed Russia to exploit its enormous resources more effectively. By the late nineteenth century, Russia might have resembled a larger version of Germany or Japan: still authoritarian in some ways, but far more industrial, educated, and militarily efficient.

This would have changed European power politics. A modernized Russia would have been much harder for Napoleon to defeat, though geography already favored Russia in 1812. More importantly, it would have performed better in the Crimean War, the Russo-Japanese War, and World War I. The humiliations that exposed Russia’s backwardness might have been avoided or softened. A stronger Russia could have dominated Eastern Europe and the Balkans more decisively, which might have frightened Britain, Austria, Germany, and the Ottoman Empire even more than historical Russia did.

Domestically, earlier modernization might have reduced the chance of the 1917 revolutions. Much of Russia’s revolutionary crisis came from the combination of autocracy, peasant land hunger, worker exploitation, military failure, and the absence of legitimate representative institutions. If Russia had developed a constitutional monarchy, a broader middle class, and legal political channels earlier, opposition movements might have become parliamentary rather than revolutionary. In that scenario, Bolshevism would probably have remained a fringe ideology rather than taking power.

But modernization could also have made unrest worse in the short term. Industrialization creates urban workers, literacy spreads radical ideas, and national minorities become more politically organized. If the state modernized economically without liberalizing politically, Russia might still have faced revolution—possibly earlier. A more efficient autocracy with factories, railways, schools, and police could have become stronger but also more repressive.

The biggest global consequence would probably be the absence, or major alteration, of the Soviet Union. Without the collapse of the Romanov state in 1917, there may have been no Bolshevik Revolution, no Leninist one-party state, no Stalinist collectivization, and perhaps no Cold War in its familiar form. Russia might instead have become a conservative constitutional empire, a nationalist great power, or a federal monarchy struggling with Poles, Finns, Ukrainians, Caucasian peoples, and Central Asians.

World War I is the major uncertainty. A modern Russia might have deterred Germany and Austria-Hungary from risking war. Or it might have made them feel encircled and strike sooner. If war still came, a better-administered, better-equipped Russia would probably have held the Eastern Front more effectively, making a Central Powers victory less likely and reducing the chance of Russian collapse.

So the most likely answer is: earlier, deeper modernization would have made Russia a much more formidable European and Asian power, reduced the likelihood of the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, and possibly produced a more stable constitutional or semi-authoritarian empire. But it would not automatically have made Russia democratic or peaceful. A modernized Russia could have become either a successful constitutional great power—or a stronger, more efficient autocracy with even greater ambitions.
